FOREWORD This Icdian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the 2nd Khadi Sectional Committee had been approved by the draft finalized by the Handlocm Textile Division Council. This standard was first published in 1962. This standard has been revised in order to overcome certain difficulties encountered by the handloom industry in implementation of this standard. Following are the important charges carried cut while revising this standard:

a) Only regative tolerances have been specified on ends/dm, picks/dm and mass g/m2 to ensure There being no tolerance on positive side on these minimum desirable construction. r t quirements, it would provide flexibility to industry to adjust construction of the fabrics depending upon market demands; on length and width have been adopted from the instructions issued by the Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry Notification No. S.O. 2937 dated 20 September 1962 under Trade and Merchandise Marks Act 1958 ( 43 of 1958 ); c) For determining the conformity of the cloth to the requirements laid down in this standard, a provision has been incorporated to allow testing of specimens in revailing atmospheric condition. However, in all cases of disputes specimens shall be tested after conditioning in the standard atmospheric conditions; and d) Provision has been incorporated for agreement between the buyer and the seller with respect of permissible number of defects in cloth. For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised)`. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.
b) Tolerance

TEXTILES - HANDLOOM VISCOSE STAPLE FIBRE SHIRTING - SPECIFICATION ( First Revision )
1 SCOPE
constructional 1.1This standard prescribes particulars and other requirements for six varieties of handloom viscose staple fibre shirting.
1.2 This standard does not specify appearance, feel, finish, etc.

n

4 MANUFACTURE 4.1 Yarn The viscose staple fibre yarn used in manufacture of cloth shall be such that the cloth produced complies with the requirements of this standard. 4.2 The cloth of varieties 1, 3, 5 and 6 shall be of plain weave and of varieties 2 and 4 in 2/2 twill weave. It shall be free from substances liable to cause subsequent tending. 5 REQUIREMENTS
5.1 The cloth shall conform

the general

However, in all cases of disputes, specimens shall be conditioned and tested in the standard atmosphere as specified in the Indian Standards referred on test methods.

ANNEX C ( Clause 6.1 )
LIST OF MAJOR FLAWS 1 One or more ends missing in the body of the material throughout its length, more than three ends missing at a place and running over 60 cm, or prominently noticeable double end running throughout the piece. 3 2 Undressed snarls noticeable over a length exceeding 5 percent of the length of the piece. 3 Smash definitely rupturing fabric. the texture of the

IS 2159 : 1991 4 Hole, cut or tear. noticeable over a 5 Reed marks prominently length exceeding 5 percent of the piece. 6 Defective or damaged selvedge noticeable over a length exceeding 5 percent of the length of the piece. 7 Skewing of more than three percent on weft. 8 Weft crack or two or more missing picks across the width of the fabric. 9 Warp or weft bar due to the difference in raw material, count, twist, lustre, colour, shade or spacing of adjacent groups of yarns ( starting mark ). 10 More than two adjacent ends running parallel, broken or missing and extending beyond 10 cm. 11 Noticeable warp or float in the body of the fabric. 12 Noticeable 14 Prominently oil or other stain in the fabric. noticeable slub.

13 Oily weft in the fabric. 15 Conspicuous broken pattern. 16 Gout due to foreign matter, usually lint or waste woven into the fabric. 17 Prominent selvedge defect. 18 Significant shading or listing in fabrics having a gradual change in one or depth of shade of hbric ( excluding selvedge or border running parallel to the selvedge ). 19 Coloured flecks. 20 Blurred or dark patch. 21 Patchy, streaky or uneven dyeing. 22 Dye bar. 23 Fuzzy appearance.

METHOD FOR DETERMINATION D-l Cut four specimens of 100 X 100 mm from a sample. Condition all the specimens in the desiccator charged with saturated solution of sodium nitrate at 27 z!z 2�C for a period of 24 hours. Remove all the specimens from the MASS OF FABRIC determine their balance to the

desiccator and immediately collective mass in weighing nearest milligram.

The Standard Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by BIS and operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a licence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards. The use of the Standard Mark is governed
